variants.title: Budget dashboard demand
variants.context: Queries per refresh = panels × queries per panel + variable queries. Steady query executions per second = viewers × queries per refresh ÷ refresh interval. Returned points scale with series, step, and range.
variants.prompt: A dashboard has 12 panels with 2 queries each and 3 variable queries. How many queries run per refresh?
variants.hint: Panels × queries per panel + variable queries.

mistakes.feedback: Multiply panels by queries per panel first.

variants.title: Budget dashboard demand
variants.context: Queries per refresh = panels × queries per panel + variable queries. Steady query executions per second = viewers × queries per refresh ÷ refresh interval. Returned points scale with series, step, and range.
variants.prompt: 20 viewers keep that 27-query dashboard open with a 30-second refresh. How many query executions per second?
variants.hint: Viewers × queries per refresh ÷ refresh interval.
variants.explanation: 20 × 27 ÷ 30 = 18 queries per second against the data source.

variants.title: Budget dashboard demand
variants.context: Queries per refresh = panels × queries per panel + variable queries. Steady query executions per second = viewers × queries per refresh ÷ refresh interval. Returned points scale with series, step, and range.
variants.prompt: A panel returns 1 point per minute. Switching the range from 1 hour to 30 days multiplies the points by how much?
variants.hint: Compare the two ranges in minutes.
variants.explanation: 30 days is 43,200 minutes; 1 hour is 60. 43,200 ÷ 60 = 720 times the points at the same step.

mistakes.feedback: Compare hours to hours: 30 days is 720 hours.

variants.title: Design for a decision
variants.context: Design around an operator question: name the decision, choose trustworthy evidence, preserve investigation context through variables and links, then test pressure and failure.
variants.prompt: A service overview is being built. Put the design steps in order.

items.text: Choose user-facing outcomes first, then dependency and resource evidence, with units and null behavior defined.
Measure load time and query demand with concurrent viewers; rehearse delayed, partial, and failed responses.
Name who uses the view and what they must decide.
Carry time range, service, environment, region, and release through variables and links.

variants.hint: Start with the decision, not the pile of available metrics.
variants.explanation: Decision → evidence → context → pressure and failure testing.

variants.title: Design for a decision
variants.context: Design around an operator question: name the decision, choose trustworthy evidence, preserve investigation context through variables and links, then test pressure and failure.
variants.prompt: An on-call drill-down is planned. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Link from the overview symptom into this view with context preserved.
State the incident decision the view supports.
Test it under concurrent viewers and data-source failure.
Select higher-resolution component evidence with bounded variables.

variants.hint: Keep the drill-down separate so diagnostic fan-out does not tax routine viewers.
variants.explanation: Every panel needs a declared question, source, unit, time context, and failure interpretation.

variants.title: Design for a decision
variants.context: Design around an operator question: name the decision, choose trustworthy evidence, preserve investigation context through variables and links, then test pressure and failure.
variants.prompt: A business-operations board is requested. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Show volume, backlog, freshness, and exceptions with owners.
Rehearse what the board shows when source data is delayed.
Preserve time and segment context through variables.
Define who acts and on what threshold.

variants.hint: Delayed source data must not hide behind a healthy-looking aggregate.
variants.explanation: A dashboard is a query client, not proof the signal is correct.

variants.title: Match the view
variants.context: A service overview answers whether the service is healthy. An incident drill-down answers why it is failing with higher-resolution evidence. A business-operations view shows volume, backlog, freshness, and exceptions with an owner.
variants.prompt: Is the service healthy right now? Which view?
options: A service overview of rate, errors, and latency.
An incident drill-down for that service.
A business-operations board with backlog.
optionFeedback: The overview answers the health question and links to investigation.
Drill-downs answer why.
Business views answer what needs action.
variants.explanation: Match the view to the job.

options: An incident drill-down with component evidence.
The service overview for that region.
A business-operations board split by region.
optionFeedback: Drill-downs carry diagnostic detail without taxing routine viewers.
The overview shows symptoms, not causes.

variants.hint: Is this a symptom or a cause question?

options: A service overview of today's traffic.
An incident drill-down on order failures.
A business-operations board with backlog and owners.

variants.title: Time the alert
variants.context: Grafana-managed rules create one alert instance per returned series. The pending period asks whether a breach persists; a recovery threshold adds hysteresis; keep firing for delays resolution. No Data and Error are not synonyms.
variants.prompt: An alert flaps every evaluation as latency crosses the threshold briefly. Which control asks whether the breach persists?
options: The pending period.
Keep firing for.
A recovery threshold.
optionFeedback: Pending requires the condition to hold for a duration before firing.
Keep firing for delays resolution, not detection.
A recovery threshold adds hysteresis on the way down.
variants.explanation: These controls solve different problems; combining long values slows both detection and recovery.

variants.title: Time the alert
variants.context: Grafana-managed rules create one alert instance per returned series. The pending period asks whether a breach persists; a recovery threshold adds hysteresis; keep firing for delays resolution. No Data and Error are not synonyms.
variants.prompt: A rule returns 400 series, so 400 alert instances fire at once. What is wrong?
options: Labels drive instance count; aggregate first.
Nothing; one instance per series is expected.
Raise the threshold so fewer series breach.
optionFeedback: One instance per returned series or dimension.
400 pages is not a signal.
The threshold is not the cause.
variants.hint: How many series does the rule query return?
variants.explanation: Aggregate before alerting; labels drive both state and notification grouping.

variants.title: Time the alert
variants.context: Grafana-managed rules create one alert instance per returned series. The pending period asks whether a breach persists; a recovery threshold adds hysteresis; keep firing for delays resolution. No Data and Error are not synonyms.
variants.prompt: The data source times out during evaluation. Is that the same as No Data?
options: Yes, a timeout returns no data points.
Yes, and both should be treated as healthy.
No. Error and No Data are separate states.
optionFeedback: A timeout means the query failed, which is not the same as an empty result.
Neither means healthy by default.
Decide each state’s behavior deliberately.
variants.hint: Did the query fail, or return nothing?

variants.title: Write source-aware queries
variants.context: Aggregate at the source, test variable interpolation with one, many, all, and empty selections, compare short and long ranges, cap unbounded series, and use the least-privileged data-source identity.
variants.prompt: A p95 panel pulls raw histogram buckets into Grafana and computes the quantile with a transformation. What is better?
options: Increase the panel refresh interval.
Compute the quantile at the source instead.
Split the work across more panels.
optionFeedback: Refresh does not fix the query shape.
Use source-native aggregation; reserve transformations for presentation.
Splitting the same raw pull across panels multiplies demand rather than cutting it.
variants.explanation: The backend executes the query; keep it efficient there.

variants.title: Write source-aware queries
variants.context: Aggregate at the source, test variable interpolation with one, many, all, and empty selections, compare short and long ranges, cap unbounded series, and use the least-privileged data-source identity.
variants.prompt: A variable-driven query works for one service but breaks when All is selected. What should have been tested?
options: Only the default single-service selection.
The dashboard time range on a long window.
Interpolation with one, many, all, and empty values.
optionFeedback: Defaults hide the failure modes.
Range comparison catches costly queries, not a broken multi-value expansion.
Interpolation changes the generated query shape.
variants.hint: What does the generated query look like with All?
variants.explanation: Inspect the generated source query before sharing.

variants.title: Write source-aware queries
variants.context: Aggregate at the source, test variable interpolation with one, many, all, and empty selections, compare short and long ranges, cap unbounded series, and use the least-privileged data-source identity.
variants.prompt: The Grafana data source is configured with an administrator database credential. What is the risk?
options: Every viewer runs queries with admin privilege.
None; Grafana permissions still gate viewers.
Slower queries from the extra privilege checks.
optionFeedback: Test authorization with the identity viewers actually use.
Grafana permissions gate panels, not what the shared credential can run.
Privilege is not performance.
variants.hint: Whose privilege runs the panel query?
